title: Decision Making
coreMove: Make the best current bet while keeping uncertainty visible enough to update when evidence changes.
sourcePressure: The chapter connects forecasting the future, poker, and Bayesian psychology to decisions under hidden information, probability, and belief-updating.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Treating good decisions as confident predictions or judging decision quality only by outcomes.

sourceAnchors.name: forecasting the future
sourceAnchors.detail: the subtitle supports forecasting as disciplined judgment about uncertainty
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: A forecast should read as a living estimate, not a promise made for pride to defend.

sourceAnchors.name: poker
sourceAnchors.detail: the subtitle supports poker as the hidden-information anchor for decisions under odds
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Poker earns its place because a good bet can still lose and a lucky result can still hide a bad read.

sourceAnchors.name: Bayesian psychology
sourceAnchors.detail: the sidecar allows Bayesian psychology as the source term for updating beliefs when evidence changes
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Bayesian psychology gives the practical discipline: change the estimate when the evidence changes.

hook: Person at a meeting realizes the real lesson
The day starts with a dashboard
counterintuition: Productivity is not doing more faster
The problem is not effort but something deeper

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person direct address, retrospective, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

exampleSpecs.domain: a fisheries analyst deciding whether to close a coastal zone after uncertain sonar readings
exampleSpecs.audience: a public-sector analyst briefing a minister
exampleSpecs.stakes: closing too early hurts boats; closing too late risks a depleted stock
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Sophie states the closure estimate as a range and names the next sonar pass that would move the recommendation
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Gray sonar bands ripple across the fisheries laptop

exampleSpecs.domain: a venture debt committee reviewing a late-stage borrower
exampleSpecs.audience: a credit officer facing a persuasive founder and partial financials
exampleSpecs.stakes: one charismatic meeting could obscure a deteriorating cash position
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Matteo separates confidence in the founder from evidence in the receivables, then updates the default probability after the new aging report
exampleSpecs.firstImage: "She sounded completely in control," one partner says

exampleSpecs.domain: a weather-dependent music festival deciding whether to delay gates
exampleSpecs.audience: an operations lead balancing crowd safety and expensive refunds
exampleSpecs.stakes: a wrong call either strands fans in storms or burns cash unnecessarily
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: At 1:35 p.m., Kiran writes the storm-delay odds on the whiteboard and marks what radar change would trigger a gate delay
exampleSpecs.firstImage: At 1:35 p.m., a green-yellow storm cell curls toward the festival map

exampleSpecs.domain: a criminal defense investigator assessing a new alibi tip
exampleSpecs.audience: an investigator trying not to overtrust a dramatic late witness
exampleSpecs.stakes: a weak update could misdirect the defense team before trial
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: It took Michael one bad tip to begin logging prior probability, source reliability, and what the tip actually changed
exampleSpecs.firstImage: It took Michael one courthouse hallway rumor to learn what a false update costs

exampleSpecs.domain: a hospital procurement team choosing whether to switch glove suppliers
exampleSpecs.audience: a procurement lead with mixed defect reports and price pressure
exampleSpecs.stakes: a cheaper contract could produce shortages or waste
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: You watch Petra revise the supplier recommendation after new defect data changes the odds, while keeping the earlier estimate visible
exampleSpecs.firstImage: You are holding two unopened glove boxes with different lot numbers

exampleSpecs.domain: a neighborhood poker night used to teach a friend about a bad business bet
exampleSpecs.audience: a small-business owner who keeps judging choices by whether the last one paid off
exampleSpecs.stakes: he may double down on a lucky but weak purchasing decision
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Anders lays out a poker hand analogy so the owner grades the purchasing decision by visible odds, not the lucky sell-through
exampleSpecs.firstImage: Was the last order smart, or did it just win the hand?
mustAvoid: letting the question hook replace the visible action beat

skillTargets: separate decision quality from outcome luck
revise beliefs without treating revision as weakness
use probability language in hidden-information situations

tryThisNowSpec: Write one live decision as a percentage estimate, then name the single piece of evidence that would move you ten points either way.
